text: The church hall smelled of floor polish and warm dust as I set my music on the piano. At rehearsal, I missed the entrance again. “Sorry,” I said, though nobody had spoken. My fingers hovered above the keys, stiff and pale, while the others turned pages and waited. I moved my chair back an inch, then another, making room no one had asked me to make. In the program draft, my name sat beneath the solo. I folded the paper until the ink disappeared inside the crease. “Maybe give that part to someone else,” I murmured. The conductor glanced up. “You know it best.” I nodded, but my stomach tightened as if I’d swallowed a stone. When the cue came, I played softly, barely above the piano’s hum. A child in the front row leaned forward to listen. I pressed the next note a little firmer.

topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Mara found the workshop key beneath a chipped flowerpot, exactly where Eli used to leave it. Inside, dust softened the outlines of his tools. She began with the shelves, wrapping each wrench in newspaper, then stopped to scrub a dark ring from the bench. The rag snagged on a splinter. She pressed her thumb against the bead of blood and watched it swell. “You always kept things in order,” she said to the empty room, too brightly. A box of bent nails slid from her hands and scattered. She crouched to gather them, moving one at a time, though the trash bin stood open beside her. Her knees ached against the concrete. On the wall, Eli’s careful pencil marks measured the height of a worktable he’d planned to build with her. Mara folded the paper over them, then unfolded it. At dusk, she carried out the tools. The box felt heavy; she held it close anyway.

topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: At 8:57, Mara stood beneath the school’s noticeboard, where the exam results were due to appear at nine. She rubbed the damp edge of her sleeve between thumb and forefinger until the cloth twisted into a cord. Around her, students joked and checked their phones. Mara kept her eyes on the blank sheet of paper, though she had read the old timetable beside it six times. When someone asked how she thought she’d done, she shrugged. “Fine,” she said, so softly he turned away before she finished. Her stomach pinched. She opened her notes app, stared at the list of people she’d promised to call, then locked the phone without choosing one. At nine, the caretaker pinned up the results. Mara searched for her name, found it, and stepped back as if the page had reached toward her. Her hands hung at her sides. She read the number again, lips moving, while the hallway filled with cheers.

topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: At the bend, the trail sign pointed toward the overlook, but I kept walking past it. The last light drained from the pines, turning the path the color of old ash. My boot caught a root. I went down on one knee and stayed there, fingers pressed into damp earth, as if waiting for the ground to tell me what to do. In my pack, the sandwich I’d made that morning was crushed flat. I took one bite, chewed twice, then wrapped it up again. “Good job,” I muttered, though nothing had happened. The words came out thin and hurried. A branch snapped somewhere behind me. I tightened every strap on my pack and stood, brushing dirt from my pants until the fabric looked no different. When the first star appeared, I checked the map, then checked it again, afraid to choose even the way back.

topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Mara set her grandmother’s flour-stained recipe card beside the mixing bowl and read the first line three times. “Two cups,” she whispered, though the kitchen was empty. She poured too much, scooped some back, then wiped the counter until the wood squeaked. The dough clung to her fingers. She scraped it off, washed her hands, and checked the card again. When the phone buzzed with a message from her brother—How’s the bread?—she turned it face down. The loaf in the oven began to rise, warm and golden behind the glass. Mara sat on the floor with her knees against her chest, listening to the timer tick. At last she pulled the bread out and pressed its crust lightly. It gave a small crackle. She cut a slice, spread butter over it, and took one bite standing at the counter. Then she wrapped the rest in a clean towel, just as her grandmother had, and sent her brother a picture.

topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: The automatic doors sighed open, and I was reaching for a dented can of soup when someone said my name. Mara stood beside the oranges, silver threads in her hair, still wearing the crooked smile I remembered from chemistry class. I dropped the can. It rolled beneath a display, clanging softly. “Look at you,” she said. “What have you been up to?” My fingers worried the frayed cuff of my sleeve. The store lights hummed above us. “A little of this and that,” I said, then laughed too quickly. She told me about her work, her house, the garden she’d planted. I nodded at all the right places, though her words seemed to arrive from the far end of an aisle. When she asked what I did, I stared at the price tag in my hand until the numbers blurred. “Nothing much,” I said. She glanced toward the checkout. I stepped aside, letting her cart pass, and went back for the soup.

text: At 11:47 on Christmas Eve, Mara wiped the counter for the fourth time, though the register had already gone dark. Her coworkers had left with paper bags of cookies and calls from home buzzing in their pockets. She folded the damp cloth into a smaller square and tucked it beneath the sink. When the manager said, “You can go,” Mara nodded, then checked the empty break room for cups no one had asked her to wash. Her hands smelled of bleach. Outside, snow blurred the streetlights; inside, the clock’s second hand clicked over and over. She took off her apron, saw a smear on it, and rubbed at the stain with her thumb. The fabric thinned beneath her nail. Her phone showed no new messages. She put it face down, straightened the chairs, and tried the door once more, though she knew it was locked.

topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The gate number changed while I was tightening my shoelace. I stood too fast, and the terminal tilted for a second. Around me, people gathered bags and hurried toward the new concourse; I tucked my boarding pass into my pocket, then checked that it was still there, then checked again. My connecting flight began boarding in twelve minutes. I jogged, my carry-on wheels rattling behind me, and clipped a man’s heel. “Sorry,” I said, though he had already turned away. At the shuttle platform, I pressed the call button twice. My palms left damp prints on my phone. When the doors opened, I stepped aside to let a family on first, then squeezed in against the wall. The screen above the seats blinked: GATE C19. I mouthed the number, afraid it might change if I looked away. At the gate, the agent asked for my pass. I fumbled, dropped it, and apologized to the floor before picking it up.

text: Mara set the paint tray on the floor and pressed a thumb into the pale blue, as if checking whether it would hold her weight. The bedroom walls were scuffed where the old dresser had stood. She rolled over each mark twice, then a third time, though the color had covered it. When the roller slipped and spotted the baseboard, she crouched at once, wiping it with her sleeve. “There. Fixed,” she murmured to the empty room. Her back ached; she kept working. At the window, dusk turned the wet paint gray. She stepped away to inspect the wall, then moved closer and found a thin streak above the outlet. The brush shook slightly in her hand. She touched it up, rinsed the brush, and left it bristles-down in the sink. The room looked clean and finished. Mara stood in the doorway, shoulders tucked in, waiting for someone to notice.

topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Rain hammered the porch roof, and I sat with my knees pulled to my chest, watching water spill from the gutter in a silver rope. I had set out a glass of lemonade before the storm; now it sat warm beside my shoe, untouched. When my sister called from inside, “Can you bring the cushions in?” I stood too fast, clipped my shoulder on the doorframe, and whispered, “Sorry,” though she hadn’t seen. I carried the cushions one at a time, squeezing them against my ribs as if they might come apart. Back on the porch, I rubbed the red mark on my arm until it faded. Thunder rolled over the houses. I tried to think of something I’d done well that day, then counted the drops racing down the railing instead. My sister laughed at something on the radio. I smiled toward the sound, careful not to make it loud enough for anyone to notice.
